title: Constant-factor online contention resolution for matroids
formal:
Is there a finite universal real constant \(C\ge1\) such that the following holds? For every finite matroid \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\), every real \(\alpha\ge1\), and every probability distribution \(D\) on \(2^E\) that admits an offline \(\alpha\)-competitive contention-resolution map, there exists a randomized online random-order strategy \(\mathcal A\) which always returns an independent subset \(S\subseteq R\) and satisfies
\[\forall e\in E,\qquad \Pr[e\in S]\ge\frac{\Pr_{R\sim D}[e\in R]}{C\alpha}.\]
Here \(R\sim D\) is the active set, the elements of \(E\) arrive in an independent uniformly random order, and the strategy learns whether an element is active only when it arrives. The strategy knows \(M,D,\alpha\) in advance; \(C\) is independent of all of them. The target is unconditional existence, without assuming the matroid secretary conjecture.

source_formulation.text: Dughmi’s ICALP 2020 §6 asks whether the unconditional conclusion of Theorem 4.1 holds: a universal online contention-resolution scheme losing a constant factor compared with offline balance. The complete target here uses the definitions in §3 and the random-order model of §4. Full knowledge of the prior and no computation restriction are retained. This replaces the previously truncated source excerpt with a fully specified statement, without turning it into a prior-independent or efficient-oracle question.

why: This question isolates the additional cost of making feasible selections online when the active set can have arbitrary correlations. Comparing with the best available offline balance avoids charging the online algorithm for distributional obstructions that already exist offline. Its constant-factor form is equivalent to the matroid secretary conjecture.
status_note: Current status checked on 16 September 2026. Singla’s arXiv:2609.14555v1, submitted 13 September, claims the general factor-four matroid secretary theorem. Through Dughmi’s published ICALP 2020 Theorem 4.1 it would imply this entire known-prior correlated contention-resolution target with C=4. The theorem/model match was checked, but the complete new proof has not been independently certified or Lean-checked here. The record is uncertain pending verification rather than source_open. The 2022 equivalence and 2025 journal abstract corroborate the relationship; efficient and prior-independent variants are separate.

progress.text: The source proves the secretary-to-contention implication and asks for its unconditional conclusion.
The sequel establishes the converse constant-factor implication, giving equivalence with the secretary conjecture.

A new preprint claims a universal factor-four secretary algorithm. If correct, the existing implication supplies a factor-four loss relative to offline contention balance. The new proof is not independently certified here.

importance.reason: A general random-order selection principle for correlated inputs, with a published equivalence to the matroid secretary conjecture and a fresh matching implication requiring verification.

sentences: A random set of active elements is drawn from an arbitrary known distribution on a finite matroid.
An offline map can inspect the whole active set before selecting an independent subset while preserving each element’s probability up to a factor alpha.
The question asks whether an irrevocable strategy seeing activity in uniformly random arrival order can always match that balance within one universal extra constant.
This known-prior correlated model is equivalent at the constant-factor level to the matroid secretary conjecture.
A September 2026 secretary proof claim would settle the target with extra factor four, so its current status awaits independent verification.

definitions:
The ground set \(E\) is finite, and \(\mathcal I\subseteq2^E\) contains \(\varnothing\), is closed under taking subsets, and satisfies augmentation: if \(I,J\in\mathcal I\) and \(|I|<|J|\), some \(e\in J\setminus I\) has \(I\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal I\). These are the matroid axioms. Elements, including loops that belong to no nonempty independent set, have fixed identities known to the strategy. Empty ground sets are allowed.

An arbitrary distribution \(D\) specifies probabilities \(D(R)\ge0\) for every \(R\subseteq E\), summing to one. Activations may be correlated in any way. An offline contention-resolution map \(\phi\) chooses a random independent subset \(\phi(R)\subseteq R\), after seeing the entire active set. Formally, it is a probability kernel from the finite set \(2^E\) to \(\mathcal I\), supported on subsets of its input. It is \(\alpha\)-competitive for \(D\) when
\[\forall e\in E,\quad \Pr_{R\sim D,\phi}[e\in\phi(R)]\ge\frac1\alpha\Pr_{R\sim D}[e\in R].\]
The premise requires the existence of such a map; the online strategy is not given its realized output or the realized set \(R\). This premise is called \(\alpha\)-uncontentiousness in the source.

First draw \(R\sim D\), a permutation \(\pi\) uniform among all permutations of \(E\), and private randomness \(U\), independently. One may represent \(U\) by a uniform seed on \([0,1]\) with measurable decisions. At step \(t\), the strategy sees only \(\pi(t)\) and the bit indicating whether \(\pi(t)\in R\), in addition to its revealed history. It must decide before the next arrival whether to select this element. Inactive elements cannot be selected. Every selected prefix must be independent, and neither acceptance nor rejection can later be reversed. The full stream contains inactive as well as active elements. The same strategy, selected from \(M,D,\alpha\), must work over all possible realized sets, orders and seeds, and may not use their future contents.

The target probability includes the active set, arrival order and private randomness. For an element with positive activation probability it is equivalently a conditional acceptance probability at least \(1/(C\alpha)\) given that the element is active; zero activation probabilities make the displayed inequality automatic. One strategy must meet the guarantee simultaneously for every element, rather than choosing a different strategy for each element. Universal means a family of strategies for all known distributions with one loss factor \(C\), not a single strategy ignorant of the prior. The model imposes no running-time, representation, sampling or oracle restriction. Exact distributional knowledge is part of the mathematical instance, and arbitrary preprocessing is permitted.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal constant-factor proposition or its full logical negation. A positive answer must establish one finite \(C\) and admissible online strategies for every promised matroid, distribution and \(\alpha\). A negative answer must show that every finite \(C\) fails on some such instance despite the existence of the stated offline map. The guarantee must hold for all elements simultaneously and all possibly correlated distributions. A theorem conditional on an unproved secretary conjecture, or a guarantee only for product distributions, does not alone establish the unconditional target. A fresh preprint claim is not itself a checked benchmark answer.

context_blocks.text: Contention resolution takes a random active subset of a ground set and retains a feasible subset while protecting the inclusion probability of every element. In a matroid, feasibility means independence. The balance guarantee is per element, so a scheme that obtains a large total cardinality while systematically discarding one active element may still fail the requirement.

The offline benchmark matters when activations are correlated. For a rank-one matroid on \(n\) elements, let \(R=E\) with probability \(1/n\) and \(R=\varnothing\) otherwise. Every element has marginal activation probability \(1/n\), but at most one element can be selected on the rare nonempty event. Even offline, simultaneous balance requires \(\alpha\ge n\). The target asks for only a constant additional loss relative to this intrinsic offline obstruction.

For product distributions, all activation indicators are independent, and classical contention-resolution results provide constant guarantees under suitable marginal feasibility. The source studies a larger class characterized by the existence of a balanced offline map, including distributions with positive correlations. Neither independent activation nor a marginal feasibility condition alone is the definition of the premise here.

Dughmi's ICALP 2020 Theorem 4.1 proves that a \(\gamma\)-competitive secretary algorithm for a matroid gives an online \(\gamma\alpha\)-competitive map for every \(\alpha\)-uncontentious distribution on that matroid. The theorem assumes the distribution is known. The paper separately discusses the difficulties of removing that knowledge and of obtaining efficient implementations; those are different questions.

The ITCS 2022 sequel proves the converse at the level of universal constants: known-prior random-order contention resolution matching offline balance up to a constant would establish the matroid secretary conjecture. Thus the unconditional target is an equivalent formulation of that conjecture, rather than merely a special case for independent random activations.

Singla's September 2026 preprint claims a secretary algorithm with factor 4 for every matroid. Combined with the published 2020 implication, this would establish this card's target with \(C=4\). This consequence uses the claimed main secretary theorem, not the separate single-sample and matroid-intersection extensions whose detailed proofs are deferred in that preprint. The current status is uncertain because this review has not independently certified the complete new proof.
